claim: Nramp family transporters are expressed in organisms from bacteria to humans.
source: Nramp family transporters—expressed in organisms from bacteria to humans—enable uptake of essential divalent transition metals via an alternating-access mechanism that also involves proton transport.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general characteristic of Nramp transporters.

claim: Nramp transporters enable uptake of essential divalent transition metals via an alternating-access mechanism.
source: Nramp family transporters—expressed in organisms from bacteria to humans—enable uptake of essential divalent transition metals via an alternating-access mechanism that also involves proton transport.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a fundamental mechanism of Nramp function.

claim: Nramp transport mechanism involves proton transport.
source: Nramp family transporters—expressed in organisms from bacteria to humans—enable uptake of essential divalent transition metals via an alternating-access mechanism that also involves proton transport.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as part of the Nramp transport mechanism.

claim: High-resolution structures of DraNramp in multiple conformations were obtained.
source: We present high-resolution structures of Deinococcus radiodurans (Dra)Nramp in multiple conformations to provide a thorough description of the Nramp transport cycle by identifying the key intramolecular rearrangements and changes to the metal coordination sphere.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that high-resolution structures in multiple conformations were obtained, and Table 1 provides resolution data (3.0 Å for G45R, 2.4 Å for G223W).

claim: Metal transport requires cycling from outward- to inward-open states in DraNramp.
source: Strikingly, while metal transport requires cycling from outward- to inward-open states, efficient proton transport still occurs in outward-locked (but not inward-locked) DraNramp.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5B showing that G223W (outward-locked) and G45R (inward-locked) showed no metal transport activity.

claim: Efficient proton transport occurs in outward-locked DraNramp.
source: Strikingly, while metal transport requires cycling from outward- to inward-open states, efficient proton transport still occurs in outward-locked (but not inward-locked) DraNramp.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5C showing that G223W (outward-locked) enabled larger basal H+ influx than WT.

claim: Efficient proton transport does not occur in inward-locked DraNramp.
source: Strikingly, while metal transport requires cycling from outward- to inward-open states, efficient proton transport still occurs in outward-locked (but not inward-locked) DraNramp.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5C showing that G45R (inward-locked) had no H+ flux.

claim: Metal and proton enter the transporter via the same external pathway to the binding site.
source: We propose a model in which metal and proton enter the transporter via the same external pathway to the binding site, but follow separate routes to the cytoplasm, which could facilitate the co-transport of two cationic species.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on structural and functional data, including the observation that inward-locked proteins do not transport either substrate.

claim: Metal and proton follow separate routes to the cytoplasm in DraNramp.
source: We propose a model in which metal and proton enter the transporter via the same external pathway to the binding site, but follow separate routes to the cytoplasm, which could facilitate the co-transport of two cationic species.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on the observation that proton transport can occur in outward-locked constructs while metal transport cannot, suggesting separate cytoplasmic pathways.

claim: The LeuT fold supports a broad range of substrate transport and conformational change mechanisms.
source: Our results illustrate the flexibility of the LeuT fold to support a broad range of substrate transport and conformational change mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the DraNramp structural and functional studies.

claim: The APC superfamily encompasses a broad range of evolutionarily-related proteins that transport diverse substrates.
source: The amino acid-polyamine-organocation (APC) superfamily of secondary transporters encompasses a broad range of evolutionarily-related proteins that transport diverse substrates including neurotransmitters, metabolites, and transition metals in organisms throughout the tree of life (Vastermark et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In humans, the APC superfamily encompasses 11 subfamilies of distinct solute carrier proteins.
source: In humans alone, the APC superfamily encompasses 11 subfamilies of distinct solute carrier proteins (Perland and Fredriksson, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The LeuT fold is the core structural unit that undergoes conformational rearrangements necessary for alternating access-based transport in the APC superfamily.
source: The LeuT fold (Yamashita et al., 2005) is the core structural unit that undergoes conformational rearrangements necessary for alternating access-based transport in the APC superfamily.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The LeuT fold consists of ten transmembrane segments divided into two pseudosymmetric, interlocking five-TM repeats.
source: This fold consists of ten transmembrane (TM) segments, divided into two pseudosymmetric, interlocking five-TM repeats, although many members have additional TMs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a structural characteristic of the LeuT fold.

claim: Primary substrates bind in a pocket formed by non-helical regions of TM1 and TM6 in LeuT-fold proteins.
source: Primary substrates bind in a pocket formed by non-helical regions of TM1 and TM6, close to the center of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a general feature of LeuT-fold proteins.

claim: Nramps enable uptake of rare micronutrients such as Mn2+ in plants and bacteria and Fe2+ in animals.
source: Natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins (Nramps) are APC-superfamily transition metal transporters that enable uptake of rare micronutrients such as Mn2+ in plants and bacteria and Fe2+ in animals (Cellier, 2012; Courville et al., 2006; Nevo and Nelson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Nramps bind and/or transport biologically-essential divalent metals such as Mn2+, Fe2+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Zn2+.
source: Nramps bind and/or transport biologically-essential divalent metals such as Mn2+, Fe2+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Zn2+—and toxic metals like Cd2+, Pb2+, and Hg2+—but not the abundant alkaline earth metals Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Bozzi et al., 2016a; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Nramps transport toxic metals like Cd2+, Pb2+, and Hg2+.
source: Nramps bind and/or transport biologically-essential divalent metals such as Mn2+, Fe2+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Zn2+—and toxic metals like Cd2+, Pb2+, and Hg2+—but not the abundant alkaline earth metals Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Bozzi et al., 2016a; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Nramps do not transport the abundant alkaline earth metals Mg2+ and Ca2+.
source: Nramps bind and/or transport biologically-essential divalent metals such as Mn2+, Fe2+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Zn2+—and toxic metals like Cd2+, Pb2+, and Hg2+—but not the abundant alkaline earth metals Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Bozzi et al., 2016a; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Metal uptake by Nramps is typically stimulated by acidic pH.
source: Metal uptake by Nramps is typically stimulated by acidic pH and accompanied by proton influx (Chen et al., 1999; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017; Gunshin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Metal uptake by Nramps is accompanied by proton influx.
source: Metal uptake by Nramps is typically stimulated by acidic pH and accompanied by proton influx (Chen et al., 1999; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017; Gunshin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Many Nramp homologs display considerable proton uniport.
source: However, many homologs also display considerable proton uniport—proton transport in the absence of added metal that suggests loose, if any, coupling between the two substrates (Chen et al., 1999; Gunshin et al., 1997; Mackenzie et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: No studies have conclusively demonstrated that Nramp is a thermodynamically coupled secondary transporter.
source: To date no studies have conclusively demonstrated that Nramp is in fact a thermodynamically coupled secondary transporter capable of harnessing a favorable gradient of metal or proton to power electrochemically-uphill transport of the other substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Nramps have 11 or 12 TMs, the first ten forming a LeuT fold.
source: Nramps have 11 or 12 TMs, the first ten forming a LeuT fold, as seen in structures of three bacterial Nramp homologs (Bozzi et al., 2016b; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017), including our model system Deinococcus radiodurans (Dra)Nramp (Bozzi et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to structural studies.

claim: Conserved aspartate, asparagine, and methionine residues in TM1 and TM6 coordinate transition metal substrates in Nramp.
source: Conserved aspartate, asparagine, and methionine residues in TM1 and TM6 coordinate transition metal substrates as observed in an inward-open state (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014), while only a metal-free outward-open state has been reported (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to structural studies.

claim: The G45R mutation mimics a human anemia-causing mutation of a conserved glycine.
source: Adding steric bulk along TM1a—for example a G45R mutation, which mimics a human anemia-causing mutation of a conserved glycine (Barrios et al., 2012)—prevented the opening of the extracellular vestibule and eliminated metal transport, emphasizing the importance of the alternating-access mechanism to DraNramp function (Bozzi et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The G45R mutation prevented the opening of the extracellular vestibule and eliminated metal transport in DraNramp.
source: Adding steric bulk along TM1a—for example a G45R mutation, which mimics a human anemia-causing mutation of a conserved glycine (Barrios et al., 2012)—prevented the opening of the extracellular vestibule and eliminated metal transport, emphasizing the importance of the alternating-access mechanism to DraNramp function (Bozzi et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: G223W eliminated Co2+ and Fe2+ metal transport in DraNramp.
source: We chose to pursue G223W—on TM6a one helical turn above the unwound metal-binding region—which like G45R eliminated Co2+ and Fe2+ metal transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: G45R fully protected the A53C inward-reporter from NEM modification, indicating an inward-locked state.
source: G45R slightly increased A53C accessibility but fully protected A61C, indicating an outward-closed state that we will refer to as inward-locked based on these data and the structure described below.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: G223W significantly increased A61C accessibility while fully protecting A53C, consistent with an outward-locked state.
source: In contrast, G223W significantly increased A61C accessibility while fully protecting A53C, consistent with an outward-locked state (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The G45R structure was determined to 3.0 Å resolution.
source: Using lipidic cubic phase (LCP) to mimic the hydrophobic membrane environment, we crystallized and determined the structures of G45R and G223W to resolutions of 3.0 and 2.4 Å, respectively, both significantly improved from our earlier DraNramp structure (3.94 Å) (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and confirmed in Table 1.

claim: The G223W structure was determined to 2.4 Å resolution.
source: Using lipidic cubic phase (LCP) to mimic the hydrophobic membrane environment, we crystallized and determined the structures of G45R and G223W to resolutions of 3.0 and 2.4 Å, respectively, both significantly improved from our earlier DraNramp structure (3.94 Å) (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and confirmed in Table 1.

claim: The G45R structure adopts an inward-occluded, metal-free state.
source: Unexpectedly, the G45R structure is not in an inward-open conformation as seen previously with our Fab-bound Patch mutant (Figure 2A) but instead adopts an inward-occluded, metal-free state (Figure 2B) that may represent an intermediate conformation between inward-open and outward-open states in the DraNramp transport cycle (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TM1a swings ~45° to partially seal the inward aqueous cavity in the G45R structure.
source: The major exception is TM1a, which swings ~45° to partially seal the inward aqueous cavity in the G45R structure, a motion we previously showed to be essential to the transport cycle (Bozzi et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis of the G45R structure.

claim: The G223W structure represents an outward-open, metal-bound state.
source: The G223W structure (Figure 2C) represents an outward-open, metal-bound state that superimposes best with the outward-open EcoNramp structure (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C and superposition analysis in Figure 2E.

claim: The G223W structure contains a bound Mn2+ in the center of the transporter.
source: As predicted, the exogenous tryptophan lines a periplasmic-facing aqueous cavity leading to a bound Mn2+ in the center of the transporter, with close helix packing below precluding metal passage to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis of the G223W structure.

claim: TMs 1, 4, 5, 6, and 10 show the largest displacements to switch metal-binding site accessibility in DraNramp.
source: Based on overall superpositions of the three DraNramp structures, TMs 1, 4, 5, 6, and 10 show the largest displacements to switch metal-binding site accessibility (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparisons shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: TMs 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, and 11 form a 'scaffold' in DraNramp.
source: The remaining TMs (2, 3, 7, 8, 9, and 11) would thus form a 'scaffold,' which adjusts to accommodate the more significant movements of the other five TMs (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: TMs 1, 4, 5, 6, and 10 do not move as a rigid body in DraNramp.
source: These matrices confirm that TMs 1, 4, 5, 6, and 10 undergo the most significant displacements relative to the rest of the protein between the different structures. But rather than moving as a rigid body such as proposed in the 'rocking bundle' model for LeuT (Forrest and Rudnick, 2009), these five TMs are also significantly displaced relative to each other.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on distance difference matrix analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the G223W outward-open structure, D56, N59, M230 and the A53 carbonyl coordinate Mn2+.
source: In outward-open DraNramp, a Mn2+ binds both D56 and M230 (2.9 and 3.0 Å), with N59 slightly further away (3.4 Å) (Figure 4A). The increased unwinding of TM6a displaces the A227 carbonyl too far (6.5 Å) to coordinate the metal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B). Instead, the A53 carbonyl coordinates the Mn2+ (2.0 Å)—our structure is thus the first to implicate this residue in the metal transport cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A with specific distance measurements.

claim: Two waters complete the Mn2+-coordination sphere in the G223W structure.
source: Two waters (2.7 and 2.8 Å) complete a Mn2+-coordination sphere.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis of the G223W structure.

claim: The G223W structure is the first to implicate the A53 carbonyl in the metal transport cycle.
source: Instead, the A53 carbonyl coordinates the Mn2+ (2.0 Å)—our structure is thus the first to implicate this residue in the metal transport cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a novel finding from the G223W structure.

claim: D56A and D56N eliminated Mn2+ and Cd2+ transport in DraNramp.
source: D56A and D56N eliminated Mn2+ and Cd2+ transport (Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D), confirming the importance of D56.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: N59A severely reduced transport of both Mn2+ and Cd2+ in DraNramp.
source: N59A severely and N59D moderately reduced transport of both metals (Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: M230A and M230T mutations affect Cd2+ more than Mn2+ transport in DraNramp.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, removing M230—the lone sulfur-containing metal-binding residue—affects Cd2+ more than Mn2+ transport, reflecting the importance of the semi-covalent interaction Cd2+ can form with sulfur (Bozzi et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Q378S and Q378N both preserved significant transport of both Mn2+ and Cd2+ in DraNramp.
source: Lastly, Q378S and Q378N both preserved significant transport of both metals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Q378 mutants increased the KM for Mn2+ but not Cd2+ in DraNramp.
source: However, these mutants increased the KM for Mn2+—but interestingly not Cd2+ (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Neither G45R nor G223W transported Mn2+, Cd2+, or Co2+ in proteoliposomes.
source: Consistent with our in vivo findings, neither G45R nor G223W transported Mn2+, Cd2+, or Co2+ (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: G223W enabled larger basal H+ influx than WT DraNramp.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of a favorable negative membrane potential established using K+ gradients and the K+-ionophore valinomycin, G223W enabled larger basal H+ influx than WT, while G45R had no H+ flux (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: G45R had no H+ flux in proteoliposomes.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of a favorable negative membrane potential established using K+ gradients and the K+-ionophore valinomycin, G223W enabled larger basal H+ influx than WT, while G45R had no H+ flux (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Adding Mn2+ did not further stimulate H+ uptake in G45R or G223W.
source: Interestingly, while Mn2+ transport stimulated H+ uptake for WT, adding Mn2+ did not further stimulate either G45R or G223W (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MTSET nearly eliminated metal transport by A61C DraNramp.
source: Charged, and thus membrane-impermeable, MTSET nearly eliminated metal transport by A61C, while uncharged NEM or MTSEA moderately impaired or did not affect transport, respectively (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), a result consistent with our previous in vivo findings that adding steric bulk, but not formal charge, is tolerated at this position (Bozzi et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MTSET-treated A61C replicated G223W's H+-transport behavior.
source: In addition, MTSET-treated A61C replicated G223W's H+-transport behavior, with higher H+ uniport compared to unmodified transporter, but little stimulation by Mn2+ (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MTSEA and NEM both eliminated metal transport by A53C DraNramp.
source: In contrast MTSET had no effect on Mn2+ and Cd2+ transport by A53C, but membrane-permeable MTSEA and NEM both eliminated transport (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transport data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MTSEA- and NEM-treated A53C resembled G45R in H+ uptake behavior.
source: Regarding H+ uptake, MTSEA- and NEM-treated A53C resembled G45R, with no basal uniport or Mn2+ stimulation, while again unmodified and MTSET-treated A53C both behaved similarly to WT (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Thrombin fully cleaved DraNramp in detergent.
source: While thrombin fully cleaved DraNramp in detergent, in proteoliposomes the cleaved protein population plateaued at ~50% (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: In proteoliposomes, the cleaved DraNramp protein population plateaued at ~50%.
source: While thrombin fully cleaved DraNramp in detergent, in proteoliposomes the cleaved protein population plateaued at ~50% (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: A network of conserved hydrophilic residues leads from the metal-binding D56 through a tight corridor between TMs 3, 4, 8, and 9 to the cytoplasm.
source: Below the metal-binding site begins a network of highly-conserved hydrophilic residues, including at least seven potentially protonatable sidechains, that leads from the metal-binding D56 through a tight corridor between TMs 3, 4, 8, and 9 to the cytoplasm (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: D56 is the only residue in the proton pathway with a pKa in the ideal 6–7 range to facilitate proton exchange at typical external pH.
source: Surprisingly, D56 is the only residue with a pKa in the ideal 6–7 range to facilitate proton exchange at a typical external pH.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on pKa calculations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: E134 has a high pKa (~11.5) indicating a near permanently-protonated state.
source: About 4 Å from D56, E134's high pKa (~11.5) indicates a near permanently-protonated state, while H232—4 Å below E134 and 7 Å from D56—has too low a pKa (~3.5) to easily protonate, as does H237 (~4.0) further down TM6b.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on pKa calculations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: H232 has too low a pKa (~3.5) to easily protonate.
source: About 4 Å from D56, E134's high pKa (~11.5) indicates a near permanently-protonated state, while H232—4 Å below E134 and 7 Å from D56—has too low a pKa (~3.5) to easily protonate, as does H237 (~4.0) further down TM6b.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on pKa calculations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Neutralizing any member of the D56-E134-H232-D131 network drastically reduced H+ transport in DraNramp.
source: Second, neutralizing any member of the D56-E134-H232-D131 network or the H237Q mutation drastically reduced H+ transport.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Mutating E124, R352, or R353 increased H+ uniport in DraNramp.
source: Third, mutating any of E124, R352, R353—farthest from D56—increased H+ uniport across multiple voltages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by proton transport data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: D56 is the likely initial protonation point in DraNramp.
source: In summary, based on our H+ transport measurements, structure-calculated residue pKa values, and prior studies using mutants of other Nramp homologs, D56 is the likely initial protonation point, with E134 and H232 positioned to chaperone the proton transfer to D131, while R352, R353, and E124 restrain this process (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on pKa calculations, mutagenesis data, and prior studies.

claim: E134 and H232 are positioned to chaperone the proton transfer from D56 to D131 in DraNramp.
source: In summary, based on our H+ transport measurements, structure-calculated residue pKa values, and prior studies using mutants of other Nramp homologs, D56 is the likely initial protonation point, with E134 and H232 positioned to chaperone the proton transfer to D131, while R352, R353, and E124 restrain this process (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on pKa calculations, mutagenesis data, and structural analysis.

claim: R352, R353, and E124 restrain the proton transfer process in DraNramp.
source: In summary, based on our H+ transport measurements, structure-calculated residue pKa values, and prior studies using mutants of other Nramp homologs, D56 is the likely initial protonation point, with E134 and H232 positioned to chaperone the proton transfer to D131, while R352, R353, and E124 restrain this process (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on mutagenesis data showing that mutations to these residues increased H+ uniport.

claim: The DraNramp mechanism differs significantly from those previously observed for other LeuT-fold transporters.
source: The mechanism described above for the DraNramp transport cycle—developed from structures of the same Nramp homolog in three distinct conformations and supported by metal and proton transport data—differs significantly from those previously observed for other LeuT-fold transporters.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional studies.

claim: In DraNramp, TMs 4, 5, and 10 join TMs 1 and 6 to form the substrate-binding 'mobile domain'.
source: In DraNramp TMs 4, 5, and 10 join TMs 1 and 6 to form the substrate-binding 'mobile domain,' while TMs 2 and 7 join the remaining TMs as part of the scaffold.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on structural analysis.

claim: TMs 2 and 7 join the remaining TMs as part of the scaffold in DraNramp.
source: In DraNramp TMs 4, 5, and 10 join TMs 1 and 6 to form the substrate-binding 'mobile domain,' while TMs 2 and 7 join the remaining TMs as part of the scaffold.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on structural analysis.

claim: The large TM1a displacement in DraNramp most closely resembles its dramatic movement in LeuT.
source: In comparison to other APC superfamily members, the large TM1a displacement in DraNramp most closely resembles its dramatic movement in LeuT (Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The DraNramp conformational changes are most similar to those predicted by comparing structures of two other bacterial Nramp homologs.
source: Not surprisingly, the DraNramp conformational changes are most similar to those predicted by comparing structures of two other bacterial Nramp homologs in complementary conformations (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017), suggesting conservation within the Nramp clade of the LeuT-fold family.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Most well-characterized LeuT-fold members are Na+-driven symporters of small organic molecules.
source: Most well-characterized members (including LeuT, BetP, and Mhp1) are Na+-driven symporters of small organic molecules which have one or two Na+-binding sites (Perez and Ziegler, 2013; Rudnick, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The Na2 site in LeuT-fold transporters consists of hydroxyls from two consecutive serines/threonines on TM8 and four main-chain carbonyls.
source: This Na2 site consists of hydroxyls from two consecutive serines/threonines on TM8 and four main-chain carbonyls (one from TM8, three from the unwound-region of TM1) (Perez and Ziegler, 2013; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The analogous location to the Na2 site in DraNramp contains highly-conserved hydroxyl-providing TM8 residues S327 and S328.
source: Intriguingly, the analogous location in DraNramp also contains highly-conserved hydroxyl-providing TM8 residues S327 (92%) and S328 (20% conserved, with another 74% as T), which may be remnants of the ancestral Na2 site conversion into a H+ site in the Nramp clade.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on sequence analysis and structural comparison.

claim: The proton-coupled amino acid transporter ApcT uses a conserved TM5 lysine (K158) as its primary proton-binding site.
source: This hypothetical evolutionary switch has precedent within the LeuT-fold family, as the proton-coupled amino acid transporter ApcT analogously uses a conserved TM5 lysine (K158), whose sidechain protrudes into the Na2 location, as its primary proton-binding site (Shaffer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: LeuT and other bacterial homologs antiport a proton as they return to an outward-open state via a conserved glutamate (E290) on TM7.
source: LeuT and other bacterial homologs also antiport a proton as they return to an outward-open state (Kantcheva et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2010; Zomot et al., 2007) via a conserved glutamate (E290) on TM7 (Malinauskaite et al., 2016), analogous to the highly-conserved N275 (100%) that lines DraNramp's intracellular vestibule.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Proton symport in ApcT and antiport in LeuT likely occur through the bulk opening and closing of the same permeation pathways used by the primary substrates.
source: Available structures and MD simulations suggest that proton symport in ApcT and antiport in LeuT likely occur through the bulk opening and closing of the same permeation pathways used by the primary substrates (amino acids) (Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012; Malinauskaite et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2009; Shi and Weinstein, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The polar network between TMs 3, 4, 8, and 9 is unique to the Nramp clade of the LeuT-family.
source: Indeed, evolutionary analysis reveals that this polar network is unique to the Nramp clade of the LeuT-family (Cellier, 2016); this region is mainly hydrophobic in both LeuT and ApcT (Shaffer et al., 2009; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The observed proton uniport in Nramp is more reminiscent of H+ shuttling in the CLC family of Cl-/H+ antiporters than the canonical Na+ transport seen in LeuT-family symporters.
source: The observed proton uniport in Nramp, requiring only subtle conformational rearrangements, is more reminiscent of H+ shuttling in the CLC family of Cl-/H+ antiporters (Accardi and Miller, 2004; Accardi and Picollo, 2010; Basilio et al., 2014; Miller, 2006) than the canonical Na+ transport seen in LeuT-family symporters.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: It remains to be demonstrated whether the observed Nramp metal and proton transport truly constitute symport.
source: It remains to be demonstrated whether the observed Nramp metal and proton transport truly constitute symport.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an open question.

claim: The DraNramp proton and metal transport mechanism is unique to the Nramp clade within the APC superfamily.
source: The DraNramp proton and metal transport mechanism we outline, where primary and driving substrates enter via a common permeation pathway but exit via separate routes to the cytoplasm—with H+ transfer perhaps triggering bulk conformational rearrangement needed for Mn2+ release to occur if the substrates are in fact coupled—is thus far unique to the Nramp clade within the APC superfamily.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional studies.

claim: The new model for Nramp transport illustrates the evolutionary flexibility and adaptability of the shared LeuT fold.
source: This new model for Nramp transport therefore illustrates the evolutionary flexibility and adaptability of the shared LeuT fold.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: DraNramp has 33% sequence identity with EcoNramp.
source: In contrast, in the recent outward-open structure of Eremococcus coleocola (Eco)Nramp (33% identity with DraNramp) the analogous glycine lines a wide aqueous channel with adequate room for tryptophan's bulk (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The G45R structure contains two protein molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: G45R contains two protein molecules in the asymmetric unit—chain A with residues 45–167 and 174–436 and chain B with residues 44–168 and 175–436 (RMSD 0.86 Å over 2899 atoms, 0.50 Å over all 386 Cαs)—and six fully or partly modeled monoolein molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the G45R structure.

claim: The G223W Mn2+-bound structure includes two Mn2+ ions—one in the metal-binding site, one at a crystal-packing interface.
source: The G223W Mn2+-bound structure includes residues 39–436, ten full or partial monooleins, one spermidine molecule, and two Mn2+ ions—one in the metal-binding site, one at a crystal-packing interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the G223W structure.

claim: The two G223W structures (Mn2+-bound and apo) align with RMSD 1.41 Å over 3012 atoms, 1.08 Å over all 398 Cαs.
source: The two G223W structures align with RMSD 1.41 Å over 3012 atoms, 1.08 Å over all 398 Cαs).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the G223W structures.

claim: An alignment of 6878 Nramp sequences was obtained from a HMMER search using the DraNramp sequence.
source: An alignment of 9289 Nramp sequences was obtained from a HMMER (Finn et al., 2011) search using the DraNramp sequence with an E-value of 1, filtered for sequences with just one domain, then filtered for sequences 400–600 residues long. Incomplete sequences and sequences lacking the canonical Nramp TM1 'DPGN' and TM6 'MPH' motifs were removed, yielding 6878 sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing sequence alignment procedures.

claim: P386 is 83% conserved in Nramp sequences.
source: Interestingly, a third proline, P386 (83% conserved), enables the top of TM10 to swing to open the metal-binding site from the periplasm, while T228 (80%) on TM6 and N426 (99%) on TM11 stabilize the extended unwound TM6 region in the G223W structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Q378 is 86% conserved in Nramp sequences, with another 11% having an N at this position.
source: In G45R, flexing of TM10 above its P386 pivot shifts Q378 (86% conserved, with another 11% of sequences, including HsNramp2, having an N at this position) ~5 Å to within hydrogen-bonding distance of metal-binding A227 and D56, perhaps stabilizing the negative charge on a deprotonated D56 during the empty transporter's return to outward-open.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: H232 is 100% conserved in Nramp sequences.
source: Highly-conserved residues surrounding the metal-binding D56 include H232 on TM6b (100% as defined) and E134 (TM3, 98%)—which have each been proposed as the Nramp proton transfer point (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017; Pujol-Giménez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence alignment analysis.

source: Intriguingly, the analogous location in DraNramp also contains highly-conserved hydroxyl-providing TM8 residues S327 (92%) and S328 (20% conserved, with another 74% as T), which may be remnants of the ancestral Na2 site conversion into a H+ site in the Nramp clade.

claim: N275 is 100% conserved in Nramp sequences.
source: LeuT and other bacterial homologs also antiport a proton as they return to an outward-open state (Kantcheva et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2010; Zomot et al., 2007) via a conserved glutamate (E290) on TM7 (Malinauskaite et al., 2016), analogous to the highly-conserved N275 (100%) that lines DraNramp's intracellular vestibule.
